title: Push-Relabel Maximum Flow
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Push-relabel avoids augmenting paths by maintaining a preflow and local height labels, with a FIFO implementation taking O(V^3) time.
short: Push excess locally and relabel stuck vertices.
long: Push excess locally and relabel stuck vertices. The highest-label variant and gap heuristics make it very fast in practice.
proof: Relabels and pushes are bounded by potential arguments over heights and excesses, giving a cubic bound for the FIFO variant.
consequence: It is a leading practical approach for large max-flow instances.

title: Bipartite Matching as a Flow Problem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Directing source-to-left and right-to-sink edges with unit capacities reduces bipartite matching to maximum flow.
short: Flow integrality automatically gives integral matchings.
long: Flow integrality automatically gives integral matchings. A unit-capacity network can be solved by Dinic in O(E sqrt(V)).
proof: Integral unit flows select a set of left-right edges with no repeated endpoint, exactly a matching.
consequence: Flow algorithms provide a general route to matching and its weighted variants.

title: Menger's Theorem and Disjoint Paths
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint paths between two vertices equals the minimum number of vertices separating them.
short: Connectivity equals the size of the smallest cut.
long: Connectivity equals the size of the smallest cut. The edge version states equality between edge-disjoint paths and edge cuts; both follow from max-flow min-cut with node splitting.
proof: Model vertex capacities by splitting vertices, apply max-flow min-cut and map integral flows to disjoint paths.
consequence: It links graph connectivity to flow and underpins network reliability analysis.

title: Node Splitting for Vertex Capacities
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Replacing each vertex v by v_in -> v_out with capacity c_v converts vertex-capacitated cuts into ordinary edge cuts.
short: Vertex limits become edge limits.
long: Vertex limits become edge limits. Incoming edges enter v_in and outgoing edges leave v_out; source and sink get infinite capacity.
proof: Any finite cut must cut a split edge to disconnect that vertex, paying exactly its vertex capacity.
consequence: It reduces minimum vertex cut and disjoint-path problems to standard max flow.

title: Gomory–Hu Cut Tree
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: An undirected graph has a weighted tree on its vertices such that the minimum cut between any pair equals the minimum edge weight on their tree path.
short: All pairwise min cuts fit in one tree.
long: All pairwise min cuts fit in one tree. It can be built with n-1 max-flow computations.
proof: Recursively find a minimum s-t cut, contract sides into tree nodes and recurse within each side.
consequence: It compactly represents global connectivity information.

title: Greedy Graph Coloring Bound
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Ordering vertices arbitrarily and assigning the smallest available colour uses at most Delta+1 colours, where Delta is the maximum degree.
short: At most Delta neighbours forbid colours at each step.
long: At most Delta neighbours forbid colours at each step. Better orderings can use fewer colours, but finding the chromatic number is NP-hard.
proof: When colouring a vertex, at most Delta colours are used by already coloured neighbours.
consequence: It is a simple constructive upper bound used in register allocation heuristics.

title: Brooks' Theorem on Chromatic Number
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A connected graph with maximum degree Delta >= 3 has chromatic number at most Delta, unless it is a complete graph or an odd cycle.
short: The naive Delta+1 bound is almost always improvable.
long: The naive Delta+1 bound is almost always improvable. The exceptional graphs indeed require Delta+1 colours.
proof: A careful greedy ordering after removing a suitable pair of non-adjacent neighbours avoids the forbidden colour at each step.
consequence: It sharpens the basic greedy bound and classifies the extremal cases.

title: Vizing's Edge Colouring Theorem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The edges of any simple graph can be coloured with either Delta or Delta+1 colours, where Delta is the maximum degree.
short: Edge colouring has only two possible answers.
long: Edge colouring has only two possible answers. Deciding which case holds is NP-hard in general, but bipartite graphs always need only Delta colours.
proof: Vizing's alternating-path argument extends a partial colouring one edge at a time.
consequence: It is a sharp structural result with applications to scheduling and matchings.

title: Eulerian Circuit Degree Characterization
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A connected undirected graph has an Eulerian circuit iff every vertex has even degree, and an Eulerian trail iff exactly zero or two vertices have odd degree.
short: You can close a tour exactly when degrees are even.
long: You can close a tour exactly when degrees are even. Each visit to a vertex consumes one entering and one leaving edge.
proof: Necessity follows from pairing arrivals and departures; sufficiency follows by Hierholzer's splicing of cycles.
consequence: It solves route-inspection and snowplough problems.

title: Hierholzer's Euler Tour Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Following unused edges until returning to the start and splicing detoured cycles produces an Eulerian tour in O(E) time.
short: Splice closed walks into a growing circuit.
long: Splice closed walks into a growing circuit. A stack of vertices with backtracking yields the tour in reverse order.
proof: Every edge is used exactly once, and splicing a closed walk at a repeated vertex preserves the Eulerian property.
consequence: It is the standard linear-time construction for Euler tours.

title: Hamiltonian Cycle Is NP-Complete
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Deciding whether an undirected graph has a Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete.
short: Finding a tour through every vertex is computationally hard.
long: Finding a tour through every vertex is computationally hard. The related travelling salesman decision problem is NP-complete as well.
proof: Membership in NP is verified by a certificate cycle; reductions from SAT or 3-SAT establish hardness.
consequence: Exact exponential algorithms and approximation heuristics are used instead.

title: Held–Karp TSP Dynamic Programming
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Subset DP computes exact shortest Hamiltonian tours in O(2^n n^2) time and O(2^n n) space.
short: Remember the best path for each visited subset and endpoint.
long: Remember the best path for each visited subset and endpoint. It is exponential but vastly better than enumerating n! permutations.
proof: dp[S][v] is the shortest path visiting exactly S and ending at v; extending by one unvisited vertex gives the recurrence.
consequence: It is the standard exact method for TSP instances with up to a few dozen cities.

title: MST Doubling Gives a 2-Approximation for TSP
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: For metric TSP, doubling an MST and shortcutting repeated vertices gives a tour of at most twice the optimum.
short: A spanning tree skeleton can be walked around cheaply.
long: A spanning tree skeleton can be walked around cheaply. The triangle inequality is needed for shortcutting not to increase cost.
proof: The doubled tree has cost 2 w(MST) <= 2 OPT, and metric shortcuts only reduce the length.
consequence: It is a simple, practical approximation guarantee for metric instances.

title: Christofides 3/2-Approximation
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: For metric TSP, adding a minimum perfect matching on odd-degree vertices of an MST yields a tour within 3/2 of optimal.
short: Fix the parity defects of the tree with a cheap matching.
long: Fix the parity defects of the tree with a cheap matching. It improves the classic 2-approximation and was the best general guarantee for decades.
proof: The matching costs at most OPT/2 by the cut and matching structure of an optimal tour, and the resulting Eulerian multigraph is shortcutted.
consequence: It is a landmark result in approximation algorithms.

title: Maximal Matching 2-Approximates Vertex Cover
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Taking both endpoints of every edge in a maximal matching gives a vertex cover of size at most twice the minimum.
short: A maximal matching certifies a near-optimal cover.
long: A maximal matching certifies a near-optimal cover. The approximation ratio is tight for this simple algorithm.
proof: Every edge of a minimum cover must touch one matched edge, so OPT is at least the matching size, while the cover has twice that size.
consequence: Vertex cover is approximable even though it is NP-hard.

title: Clique and Independent Set Complementarity
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A set is a clique in G exactly when it is an independent set in the complement of G.
short: Cliques and independent sets are the same problem in complementary graphs.
long: Cliques and independent sets are the same problem in complementary graphs. Both problems are NP-complete, and both are hard to approximate within n^{1-epsilon}.
proof: Adjacency is inverted in the complement, so pairwise adjacency becomes pairwise non-adjacency.
consequence: Reductions between the two problems are immediate.

title: Graph Isomorphism Complexity Status
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Graph isomorphism is in NP but is not known to be in P or NP-complete; Babai gave a quasipolynomial-time algorithm.
short: Its complexity sits in a rare unresolved middle ground.
long: Its complexity sits in a rare unresolved middle ground. Practical tools use refinement and backtracking, such as the Weisfeiler–Leman hierarchy.
proof: A permutation mapping is an easily verified certificate, and Babai's group-theoretic algorithm runs in exp((log n)^{O(1)}) time.
consequence: It is a central open problem with implications for symmetry detection and chemistry.

title: Bitset Transitive Closure
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Representing reachability rows as bit vectors computes the transitive closure in O(n^3 / w) machine operations for word size w.
short: Warshall's update becomes a bitwise OR.
long: Warshall's update becomes a bitwise OR. The space is O(n^2 / w) words, and it is fast for moderate n on 64-bit machines.
proof: Row update R[i] |= R[k] whenever R[i][k] is set operates on w bits at once.
consequence: Bitset acceleration makes dense reachability queries practical.

title: Repeated Squaring for Reachability
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The Boolean adjacency matrix raised to the n-th power under Boolean matrix multiplication gives the transitive closure.
short: Matrix powers count walk lengths.
long: Matrix powers count walk lengths. Repeated squaring needs O(log n) Boolean matrix products, each reducible to fast matrix multiplication.
proof: An entry of A^k is 1 exactly when a walk of length k exists, and any reachable pair has a walk of length at most n-1.
consequence: It links reachability to the theory of fast matrix multiplication.

title: Planar Graph Edge Bound
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A simple planar graph with n >= 3 vertices has at most 3n - 6 edges, and at most 2n - 4 if it is bipartite.
short: Euler's formula limits how dense a planar graph can be.
long: Euler's formula limits how dense a planar graph can be. Consequently planar graphs are sparse and admit efficient algorithms.
proof: Euler's formula n - m + f = 2 and the fact that each face has at least 3 (or 4) sides give the inequality.
consequence: Planarity implies linear space and often linear-time algorithms.

title: Linear-Time Planarity Testing
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The Hopcroft–Tarjan algorithm tests planarity and produces an embedding in O(V) time.
short: Depth-first search structure characterises embeddability.
long: Depth-first search structure characterises embeddability. It relies on partitioning DFS edges into interlacement classes to check whether conflicts can be resolved.
proof: The algorithm constructs an embedding incrementally and proves that any failure implies non-planarity by Kuratowski's theorem.
consequence: Planarity can be recognised as cheaply as reading the graph.

title: Five Colour Theorem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Every planar graph can be coloured with at most five colours.
short: Euler's formula guarantees a low-degree vertex for induction.
long: Euler's formula guarantees a low-degree vertex for induction. The four-colour theorem strengthens this to four but has a much harder proof.
proof: A planar graph has a vertex of degree at most 5; removing it, colouring recursively and using Kempe chains handles the degree-5 case.
consequence: It gives an elementary colouring guarantee for maps and planar networks.

title: Bipartite Edge Colouring Needs Delta Colours
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Every bipartite graph has an edge colouring with exactly Delta colours, where Delta is the maximum degree.
short: Bipartite structure eliminates Vizing's extra colour.
long: Bipartite structure eliminates Vizing's extra colour. Such a colouring can be found in polynomial time by repeated matching on a regularised graph.
proof: Embed the bipartite graph in a Delta-regular bipartite multigraph, decompose into Delta perfect matchings by Hall's theorem and restrict.
consequence: It yields optimal timetabling for bipartite conflict structures.

title: Minimum Cut for Image Segmentation
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Binary image segmentation can be formulated as an s-t minimum cut where unary terms attach pixels to labels and pairwise terms penalise label disagreements.
short: Graph cuts optimise a common vision energy.
long: Graph cuts optimise a common vision energy. Submodular pairwise terms make the energy exactly minimisable by max flow.
proof: The cut capacity equals the sum of unary and pairwise costs under the standard construction, so a minimum cut minimises the energy.
consequence: Max-flow algorithms are core tools in computer vision.
wiki: Graph cuts in computer vision and artificial intelligence

title: Offline Dynamic Connectivity over Time
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: For a known sequence of edge insertions and deletions, a segment tree over time intervals with rollback union-find answers connectivity queries in O(E log T alpha(V)).
short: Assign each edge to time segments and process recursively.
long: Assign each edge to time segments and process recursively. Rollback union-find restores state when backtracking, avoiding persistent copies.
proof: Each edge appears in O(log T) segment-tree nodes; at a leaf all active edges have been unioned exactly once.
consequence: It solves dynamic connectivity efficiently when the whole update sequence is known in advance.
